original_value: AbstractWe present two studies evaluating the effectiveness of flagging inaccurate political posts on social media. In Study 1, we tested fact-checker flags, peer-generated flags, and a flag indicating that the publisher self-identified as a source of humor. We predicted that all would be effective, that their effectiveness would depend on prior beliefs, and that the self-identified humor flag would work best. Conducting a 2-wave online experiment (N = 218), we found that self-identified humor flags were most effective, reducing beliefs and sharing intentions, especially among those predisposed to believe the post. We found no evidence that warnings from fact checkers or peers were beneficial. Compared to the alternatives, participants exposed to self-identified humor flags exhibited less reactance to and had more positive appraisals of the flagging system. The second study (N = 610) replicated the findings of the first and provides a preliminary test of what makes this flag work.

result.paraphrase: Abstract: We report two studies assessing how well social-media flags work for inaccurate political posts. Study 1 compared fact-checker flags, peer-generated flags, and a flag stating that the publisher self-identified as a source of humor. We expected all three to help, that effects would vary with prior beliefs, and that the self-identified humor flag would be most effective. In a two-wave online experiment (N = 218), the self-identified humor flag proved most effective, lowering belief in the post and intentions to share it, particularly among participants already inclined to believe it. We found no evidence that fact-checker or peer warnings were helpful. Relative to the other conditions, those exposed to the self-identified humor flag showed less reactance and rated the flagging system more positively. Study 2 (N = 610) replicated Study 1 and offered an initial test of why this flag works.
